questions.scenario: A 240-person engineering organisation is rolling Claude Code out. The platform team can enforce centrally managed settings, publish plugins and manage MCP servers; it cannot dictate which model an individual engineer chooses. Security has approved a written standard that says which capability groups each team may use and what data may not be sent. Four teams have already asked for exceptions.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible split between what should be standard across the organisation and what should stay with teams?

options.text: Standardise everything, including conventions and prompt structure. Consistency across 240 engineers reduces review load and makes the rollout legible to leadership, and the teams can still override locally.

Standardise the boundaries and decentralise the working practice. Enforce centrally what carries organisational risk — which data may leave, which tools are permitted, which actions need a human, and which model families are approved — because those are the things where one team's shortcut becomes everyone's exposure. Leave the day-to-day working practice with teams: their conventions, their test commands, their review habits. Then publish the standard as something teams comply with rather than something they configure.
Standardise nothing centrally and publish the written standard as guidance. A platform team that configures 240 engineers' tools becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
Standardise only what teams ask for most often, and revisit quarterly. Fixing the standard from demand rather than from risk means the highest-risk use cases are the ones nobody has asked about yet.

questions.explanation: The organising principle is **risk versus reversibility**. Data leaving the organisation, the permitted tool surface, the actions that need a human and the approved model families are hard to reverse, hard to attribute and uniform in their consequences — so they belong where they can be enforced uniformly, and a written standard alone cannot enforce them. Conventions and working practice are cheap to vary, cheap to correct in review, and locally specific: standardising them buys tidiness at the cost of the platform team becoming a bottleneck. Both halves are enforceable; only one of them is standardised.

whyWrong.A: This conflates two different things and asks teams to override the standard they were just given, which is not consistency. It also standardises the least valuable layer while leaving the high-risk boundaries merely written down.
whyWrong.C: A written standard with no enforcement is the option that produced the two-month rollout drift in the comparable programmes. The boundary is exactly the category where guidance reliably fails, because the failure mode is individual and the benefit is collective.
whyWrong.D: Demand-driven standardisation is where the exposure goes. The teams least likely to ask for a capability are frequently the ones handling the most sensitive data, so the request queue is a poor guide to what needs a boundary.

questions.mindset: Centralise what is irreversible and organisation-wide; leave the reversible, locally specific working practice with the teams.

questions.scenario: Kestrel Group's platform team maintains the shared configuration for about 40 repositories: an instruction file per service, four skills, three subagents and a hook set. Changes arrive as one-line edits from individual teams. Last quarter three services ended up with contradictory conventions, and one hook was silently dropped from eleven repositories when someone copied a folder by hand.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about how the shared configuration should be maintained are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Treat the shared configuration as production code: one source, changes as reviewed pull requests with a named owner, a stated rollout order across repositories, and a stated rollback. The problem in the scenario is not that copies exist — it is that nothing governed how they are made or retired.
Centralise everything in a single organisation-wide file and reference it from every repository, so there is only one copy to keep correct.

Keep the per-service configuration separate and distribute it through a mechanism that the platform team owns, rather than by copying folders between repositories. Copying is what produced the eleven repositories where a hook silently disappeared and nobody could say when.
Let each service diverge. The conventions that matter to one service are rarely right for another, so forcing consistency is the root cause.

questions.explanation: Two things are true at once, and they are about different layers. **Governance** of the change is what was missing: three contradictions and eleven silently drifted copies are what one-line edits and hand-copied folders produce, so review with an owner, a rollout order and a rollback treats the artefact as what it has become. And **distribution** is what removes the copying: per-service configuration is right, delivered through a mechanism the platform team owns. Merging everything into one organisation-wide file is the wrong shape, because it forces service-specific conventions to read as if they were general.

whyWrong.B: A single organisation-wide file is the wrong shape for service-specific conventions, and a reference from every repository re-creates the drift in a new form: each repository now has a reference line and nothing guarantees the thing referenced is present or current.
whyWrong.D: Some divergence is legitimate, and this option names a real problem. It uses it to justify no governance at all, which is what produced the eleven drifted copies. The answer is per-service conventions with governed distribution, not abandonment.

questions.mindset: Duplication is not the disease — ungoverned change and hand-copied distribution are. Review the change and own the distribution.

questions.scenario: Ardenne Foods ran a six-week AI-assisted development trial on two teams of similar size. Team A had a mature setup: a documented build and test loop, clear conventions, and a reviewer who read every diff. Team B had nothing beyond the tooling. Team A's cycle time fell 18% and its escaped defects held flat. Team B's cycle time fell 9% and its escaped defects rose by a third. Both teams were measured on the same four metrics.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible reading, and what does it imply for the rollout?

options.text: The tooling produced a 9% improvement even in the worst conditions, so the answer is to roll it out everywhere immediately and address quality practices separately.
Team B's defect increase proves the tooling reduces quality, so the 18% figure should be discounted as an outlier.

The tooling is not the variable that differed — the surrounding engineering practice was, and Team A's result shows what is achievable while Team B's shows what happens without it. The implication is that enablement and fast feedback are part of the deliverable, not a follow-up activity, and that teams without them should be sequenced later rather than left to discover the problem.
The comparison is inconclusive because the two teams were not randomly assigned, so neither figure should be used to justify a rollout.

questions.explanation: The most useful thing in the evidence is the **contrast between two teams using the same tooling**, because that isolates the surrounding practice as the variable. Team A's numbers say the ceiling is real and quality can hold; Team B's say the tooling alone does not deliver it. That converts an argument about the product into a sequencing and enablement decision — which is actionable now, and it explains the defect increase rather than leaving it as noise.

whyWrong.A: This reads the weaker team's throughput gain as the floor and treats quality as a separate workstream. Team B's escaped defects rose by a third while the review burden went with it, and the cost lands after the rollout window has closed.
whyWrong.B: Two teams with the same tooling and different outcomes is evidence about the surrounding practice, not about the tooling. Discarding the 18% figure because one team did badly removes the best evidence the organisation has about what good looks like.
whyWrong.D: Random assignment is the gold standard and is rarely available. The comparison here is between two teams that differed in exactly one hypothesised way, which is enough to justify the sequencing decision that follows.

questions.mindset: When two teams share the tooling and get different results, the variable is the surrounding practice — that is your sequencing decision.

questions.scenario: Verity Health's platform team has added an automated reviewer that runs on every AI-assisted pull request. Reviewer complaints have risen: developers say the comments restate what the diff already shows. The team measured that developers act on about 4% of the comments and that review time per pull request is up 22%.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful next move?

options.text: Remove the automated reviewer. If developers act on 4% of its comments, the 22% review-time increase is not justified.
Keep the reviewer but make it run only on pull requests above a certain size, so reviewers spend less time on small changes.
Keep the reviewer and ask developers to respond to every comment, so the comments get the attention they deserve.

Change what the reviewer is for rather than how often it runs. Restrict it to findings with a consequence — correctness, security, a missed test, a regression risk — and require each comment to name the specific line and the reason it matters. The current 4% action rate and 22% time increase are the measurement of a reviewer producing low-value output, and volume is not the variable.

questions.explanation: A 4% action rate with a 22% review-time cost is a **precision problem**, and the remedy is to make the output worth acting on: findings with a consequence, anchored to a line and justified. Cutting volume by size threshold does not address it, because a large pull request is just as capable of producing four useful comments. Making developers respond to low-value comments converts a review cost into a reply cost, which is worse.

whyWrong.A: The two numbers describe the current reviewer, not the idea of automated review. Removing it discards the 18% of AI-assisted changes that were caught mechanically, which are the ones no human reviewer reliably finds.
whyWrong.B: A size threshold reduces cost without improving precision, so the comments developers do act on stay the same and the ones they ignore stay too. It also exempts the largest changes, which are where a mechanical finding is most valuable.
whyWrong.C: Requiring a response to every comment makes developers write to dismiss them. The 4% action rate is a signal about the content of the comments, not about developers' diligence.

questions.mindset: A low action rate with a rising review cost is a precision problem, so raise the value of a finding rather than its frequency.

questions.scenario: Thurloe Water's engineering leadership wants one skill that covers its incident response process. The incident process is about 30 steps and changes every quarter. Someone proposes writing it as a skill so every on-call engineer runs the same steps in the same order.

options.text: A 30-step process is well beyond what a skill should contain, so it belongs in the instruction file instead, where engineers can read it before every incident.

Follow the frequency, not the length. The process changes quarterly and is used in high-stakes conditions a few times a month, so the cost of it being quietly out of date is high and the number of times it is used is low. A skill's value comes from being invoked automatically in the situation it covers, and it needs an owner and a review cycle to stay correct. Some of the process belongs in a skill; the version ownership and the quarterly review do not.
The process is a good candidate for a skill and needs no governance beyond a quarterly review, because a skill is versioned with the repository like any other file.
Incident response should not be assisted at all. Under pressure, following documented steps with a colleague is more reliable than following them with a tool.

questions.explanation: The deciding variables are **how often it runs and what a stale version costs**. Quarterly changes against a monthly usage means most invocations could use an out-of-date process, in the situation where being wrong is most expensive. That makes ownership and a review cycle part of the deliverable rather than an afterthought — a skill is a mechanism that fires on its own, and an unowned one drifts silently. It does not follow that the skill is wrong, only that its governance has to be designed.

whyWrong.A: Length is not the criterion, and instruction files are read when the model is told to read them rather than invoked because the situation matched. For a low-frequency process that changes, automatic invocation at the right moment is the main argument for the skill in the first place.
whyWrong.C: This acknowledges the review but treats it as sufficient. The gap is ownership: a review has to have someone responsible for performing it, and quarterly is an assertion about cadence rather than an answer to who checks that the process still matches reality.
whyWrong.D: The finding is reasonable and the conclusion is not. Assistance that surfaces the current checklist during an incident is different from replacing judgement, and most incident failures are omissions under time pressure rather than failures to follow a documented sequence.

questions.mindset: Size a guidance artefact by how often it runs and what staleness costs — and an unowned artefact that fires on its own will drift.

questions.scenario: Marchmont Energy measures four signals across its AI-assisted pipeline: pull-request cycle time, the share of AI-assisted changes needing a second pass for tests, the number of reviewers per change, and the time from a merge to a production incident. Nine months in, cycle time is down 20%, the second-pass rate is up 15 points, reviewer count per change is up 40%, and incident count is unchanged.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible conclusion for a leadership review?

options.text: Cycle time down 20% with incidents unchanged is a clear success, and the extra review is the cost of catching what would otherwise have shipped.
The 15-point rise in second-passing shows a quality regression that invalidates the cycle-time gain, and the rollout should be paused until the second-pass rate returns to its previous level.

Delivery improved and review capacity did not keep pace; the pipeline is producing change faster than the organisation can absorb it, and quality held only because reviewer count rose to match. The number to watch is the second-pass rate and review time, and the remedy is review capacity and test conventions rather than more tooling.
No conclusion is supportable because reviewer count and second-pass rate are not measures of quality, and leadership should be given only cycle time.

questions.explanation: The four signals describe one system, and they are consistent with a single explanation: **throughput rose, review load rose with it, and incidents held flat because the extra review absorbed the difference**. That is a real capacity finding rather than a contradiction — a 40% rise in reviewers per change is the organisation paying to keep the same quality. It names a specific remedy and a specific metric to track, which is what a leadership review needs.

whyWrong.A: Incidents unchanged is not independent evidence of success here, because review effort rose at the same time. Reading the incident count as a quality verdict treats a compensating control as a free improvement.
whyWrong.B: Incidents did not rise and the second pass is a measure of work in progress, not of what reached production. Pausing the rollout over a metric that the extra review is designed to produce would remove the compensating control while keeping the throughput.
whyWrong.D: Second-pass rate and reviewer count are exactly what a delivery organisation should be measuring, and they are the numbers that reveal the capacity constraint. Stripping them out of the review leaves leadership with a number that cannot be acted on.

questions.mindset: When throughput rises and review load rises with it while incidents hold flat, name the capacity constraint rather than claiming either success or failure.

questions.scenario: Wrenfield Logistics runs an overnight job that produces migration scripts from a staging copy of production. Twice, a script generated by the job has failed against production with an error that a test on the staging copy could not have caught. The engineering lead's first instinct is to add a review step for generated scripts.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about how to investigate this are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: A staging copy cannot reproduce the condition, so more validation on staging raises confidence in the wrong thing. Establish what is actually different between staging and production — data distribution, volume, a constraint, a concurrent workload — and then either make the job test against that difference or stop it running unattended against production at all.
The right fix is the review step. Generated code deserves the same scrutiny as any other change, and a human reviewer would have caught the error before production.

The evidence also limits what the successful runs prove. Earlier runs against the same staging snapshot are not evidence that the job is reliable against production, so the honest conclusion is that the job is unvalidated rather than that it mostly works.
Investigate whether the model hallucinated the failing step. If the step was in the input, the behaviour is defensible given the input.

questions.explanation: The evidence says the **verification environment cannot reach the failure condition**, which is a different problem from insufficient scrutiny, and it follows that earlier passes against the same snapshot are not evidence of reliability. A review step improves the chance that a person notices a problem the job produced; it does not produce the missing signal, and the reviewer assembles their context from the same stale snapshot.

whyWrong.B: This addresses attention rather than information. A reviewer sees the generated script and whatever context they assemble themselves, and the failures were by definition not reproducible on staging — so the review may well pass the script that fails in production.
whyWrong.D: The question of whether the step was hallucinated is worth asking and is cheap to answer, but it is not where the investigation should stop. A step that was in the input is still a step that will fail in production, and the failure is in what the job was validated against.

questions.mindset: If verification cannot reproduce the failure, more scrutiny on the same artefacts will not help — find what the environment is missing.

questions.scenario: Oakhurst Housing's on-call engineer used Claude Code during a database incident. The session produced three plausible explanations, all of which were wrong. The engineer could not tell afterwards which inputs had been used, in what order files were read, or what the tool actually returned — only the conversation.
questions.stem: Which change would MOST improve the next incident of the same kind?

options.text: Require the engineer to verify each hypothesis against the production telemetry before adopting it. That is the control that would have caught all three.
Use a stronger model for incident work. Three wrong hypotheses from a capable model is a sign the inputs were wrong, not that the reasoning was weak.
Stop using an assistant during incidents. Ambiguity plus time pressure is exactly the condition the guidance describes as inappropriate for unsupervised work.

Capture the session as a durable artefact — tool calls, arguments and results — in a place the engineer can read afterwards, so a hypothesis can be checked against what was actually examined. The conversation shows reasoning; it does not show evidence, and that is the specific thing missing here.

questions.explanation: The engineer lost **evidence, not judgement**. The conversation records what was concluded and in what order it was reasoned, but a hypothesis that was never checked against a log or a metric looks identical in the transcript to one that was. Making tool calls and their results durable as a record is what lets the next engineer — or the same one an hour later — see whether the basis existed. That is a change to the evidence available, not to how carefully someone reasons.

whyWrong.A: This is right in principle and addresses a different gap: it asks for more care in the moment rather than making the moment auditable. It would not have helped the engineer who could not reconstruct what had been examined.
whyWrong.B: A stronger model given the same inputs produces the same class of answer. The hypotheses were wrong because the evidence was not there, which is an information problem and not a capability one.
whyWrong.C: The conclusion is defensible for unattended use but does not fit this case: the engineer was present, verifying, and the tooling helped. What was missing was a record, not the absence of the tool.

questions.mindset: After an incident, ask what evidence is missing — a conversation records reasoning, not what was examined.

questions.scenario: Selwyn Energy's shared configuration was updated centrally on a Thursday afternoon. By Friday morning, engineers across nine repositories reported that suggestions ignored their project conventions. The change was correct and had been reviewed; nothing had been reverted.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful characteristic of this change for the organisation to build in?

options.text: A mandatory approval from two senior engineers on every configuration change. The change was correct, so more review would not have prevented the incident.

A rollback path and a canary order, not more review. This change was already correct and reviewed, so the defect is blast radius and time-to-recover rather than decision quality: roll it out to one repository, observe, then proceed — and be able to revert centrally in one action rather than one repository at a time. Central distribution makes both possible, which is part of the reason to centralise.
An announcement to all engineers before the change lands, so nobody is surprised. Nine teams found out from behaviour rather than from a message.
A version pin on each repository's configuration, so repositories cannot be changed centrally again. Central control is what caused this.

questions.explanation: The change was **correct and reviewed**; what it lacked was a way to limit how far it spread before anyone noticed, and a way to undo it quickly. Central distribution is what makes both available — a canary repository first, and one revert action rather than nine repository edits. This is the strongest practical argument for centralised configuration, since a distributed equivalent has neither property.

whyWrong.A: The scenario states the change was correct and had been reviewed. Adding a second approver to a change that turned out to be right addresses decision quality, which was not the defect.
whyWrong.C: An announcement makes the change legible but does not reduce blast radius or shorten recovery. The teams who were affected behaved reasonably — they reported it rather than working around it.
whyWrong.D: Removing central control makes each fix a change in nine repositories, which is slower to roll out and slower to undo. The failure was in how a correct change was rolled out, not in having central control.

questions.mindset: A correct change can still be a bad rollout — canary the blast radius and keep a one-action rollback.

questions.scenario: Pennington Water's support organisation had a bad experience with an AI-assisted deployment in production. A change was approved, deployed and caused a customer-visible outage for 40 minutes. The post-incident review found the change was technically correct, matched the specification, and passed every automated check. It was simply the wrong change for that moment.
questions.stem: Which TWO process changes are MOST defensible? Choose TWO.

options.text: Treat this as a judgement failure rather than a testing failure, and change what is decided rather than what is checked. The evidence is that every automated gate passed and the outcome was still wrong, so more gates of the same kind add cost without addressing the failure.
Add a staging soak period before promotion. The change passed every automated check immediately, and a window in which nothing bad happens is evidence the promotion decision was premature.

Change the boundary on consequential actions — canary rollout, a named approver for changes a customer can see, and an explicit statement that a passing check is evidence for a decision rather than the decision itself.
Ban assisted changes to production entirely, so the class of failure cannot recur.

questions.explanation: Every automated gate passed and the change was still wrong, which locates the failure in **whether it should have gone out then**, not in whether it was correct. So the diagnosis and the remedy point the same way: treat it as a judgement failure, and change the decision boundary rather than adding checks of a property the change already satisfied. Bounding exposure — canary, a named approver — is the specific form that takes for an action a customer can see.

whyWrong.B: A soak period is a plausible instinct and a weaker control here. The review found the change matched the specification, so the defect was not that it needed more time to be detected; and a window in which nothing bad happens is weak evidence about the decision to promote.
whyWrong.D: A blanket ban removes the capability rather than the exposure. If the team cannot change production responsibly, the honest conclusion is about the decision boundary and the rollout, not about the tool.

questions.mindset: When every automated gate passes and the outcome is still wrong, the defect is authorisation and exposure, not testing.

questions.scenario: Calverton Foods' team spends about a day a week reading the same file. The engineer using Claude Code has asked several times for the content to be summarised into a notes file instead of re-read every session. The file is roughly 900 lines and changes about once a fortnight.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful advice to give?

options.text: Summarise the file once and store the summary next to it, then point the session at the summary. That removes the 900 lines from every session at no cost.
This is expected. A repository of this size costs about that much context, and the summary will drift from the source within a fortnight, so reading the real file each time is the safer choice.

Treat the file the way to handle the fact it represents. If the reason it is read every session is that the agent needs to know current status, that is a small piece of durable state with an owner and a refresh, and it belongs where it is written down and read on demand rather than re-derived from a 900-line file on every session. Before summarising, though, find out whether the file is being read to answer a question that a status field would answer directly.
Move the file into the project instruction file so it is always loaded. If it is needed every session, it belongs where every session can see it.

questions.explanation: A day a week on one file is a **signal about what the work actually needs**, and the first useful question is what the sessions are reading it for. If the answer is 'current status', then the real content is a handful of fields with an owner and a refresh, and that is a different artefact from a 900-line document. A summary is the fallback once you know what the summaries are for — and it is the wrong answer here if the need is a live value rather than prose.

whyWrong.A: Summarising a file that changes fortnightly creates a second artefact to keep correct, and 'no cost' is not accurate for an ongoing sync. The cheaper design is to reduce what is needed, not to copy what is not.
whyWrong.B: The drift concern is real but it is being used to defend the status quo at an unaffordable cost. Re-reading is the expensive option, and the drift risk of a summary is manageable because the refresh is a known event rather than an unbounded read every session.
whyWrong.D: Instruction files are standing context read on every turn for every task, including the majority of tasks that have nothing to do with this file. That makes it a worse home for a large document than a file read on demand.

questions.mindset: When one file dominates the week, the answer is usually that the work needs a status rather than a document — find out before summarising.

questions.scenario: Fenwick Motors' engineering lead has been given a task from the CFO: cut the time spent writing supplier quality reports. The lead has 90 days. The reports are produced from data the team already has, follow a template, and about 40 are written a quarter. The lead asks whether to build an automated pipeline or have the team use the existing tooling better.
questions.stem: Which TWO parts of the recommendation are MOST defensible? Choose TWO.

options.text: Recommend improving the existing approach first, and say why in business terms. The work is fixed-shape and already understood by the people doing it, so drafting from existing data with a shared template and a review step needs no new service, no new owner and no new failure modes.
Recommend the automated pipeline. Ninety days is enough time to build it, and it removes the work from the team entirely, which is what the CFO asked for.

Set a checkpoint at 30 days against the same measures, and say a pipeline is a reasonable second step if drafting alone does not move the number. That gives the sponsor a decision point instead of a delay.
Recommend neither, and tell the CFO the measurement cannot support the claim. Without a baseline for the 40 reports, any saving is unverifiable.

questions.explanation: The work is **fixed-shape and already understood by the people who do it**, which is the strongest signal to improve the existing approach rather than build a service. What makes this defensible in a stakeholder conversation is that it is not 'do nothing' — it is a change with a date, a measure and a defined next step, plus an honest statement of what a pipeline would add: a new component, a new owner and a new set of ways to be wrong. Framing it that way gives the sponsor a decision point instead of a delay.

whyWrong.B: Ninety days is a constraint, not a reason to prefer the heavier option, and 'removes the work entirely' is a promise the pipeline would not keep — the review step remains either way. It also commits the team to a component they will own for years to solve a problem whose first step is cheap.
whyWrong.D: The measurement objection is fair and has an answer: record the current time for a handful of reports in week one. Declaring the task unverifiable avoids a conversation the team can actually have.

questions.mindset: For well-understood fixed-shape work, propose the cheap change with a date, a measure and a defined next step — not a refusal to build.

questions.scenario: Redhaven Group's platform team has spent a quarter standardising tooling across the estate and has little to show for it. They surveyed engineers: 40% had never opened the shared configuration, and those who had rated the usefulness 3 out of 10. The team wrote the documentation; the documentation is thorough.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful diagnosis?

options.text: The team solved distribution and documentation and not the first five minutes. If 40% have never looked at it, the question is not whether they read it but whether they ever encountered a moment where it would have helped — and whether it helped when they did. The cheap interventions are to put the guidance where a task starts and to make the shared configuration visible in the repository rather than in a place people have to know about. Content quality is downstream of being found.
The documentation is too long. Engineers rated it 3 out of 10 because there was too much to read, so it should be cut to a single page.
The rollout needed more communication. A quarterly town hall and a summary email would reach the 40% who never opened it.
The standard was wrong. Three out of ten from people who read it indicates the content itself does not match how the teams work, so it needs rewriting from scratch.

questions.explanation: The survey result has two parts and they point in one direction: **40% never opened it, and those who did rated it 3 out of 10**. The second number cannot be explained away by discoverability alone, and the first cannot be explained away by quality — a document nobody opened was never judged. So both are live, and the cheap order is to fix finding it before rewriting it, because content work on an artefact that is not being reached will not show up in the rating. Putting guidance where a task begins is what changes the 40%.

whyWrong.B: Cutting to one page addresses length, which is not the finding. Forty percent never opened the document at all, so length cannot be why they did not.
whyWrong.C: More communication is more of the same channel that has already not worked for 40% of the estate. The finding is about where guidance is encountered during work, not about how often the team announces it.
whyWrong.D: This reads the 3 out of 10 as a verdict on the content and skips the harder half of the evidence. A rating from people who found it is worth taking seriously — but the response is to test it on a task, not to conclude from one number that a quarter of work should be discarded.

questions.mindset: When nobody opened it and everyone who did rated it low, fix finding it before rewriting it — and verify the content on a real task.

questions.scenario: Cavendish Retail's AI-assisted pipeline writes migration scripts that a service owner then runs by hand. Three migrations have been written and applied successfully. A fourth arrived with a step that reads from a table the owner has never seen in the schema, and the owner stopped and asked. The pipeline's logs show the step came from a table present in a staging snapshot that no longer exists in production.
questions.stem: What is the MOST useful next step?

options.text: Treat this as a data-environment defect and separate the two things that were conflated. The pipeline was validated against a snapshot that no longer matches production, so its output is not evidence about production — and a human reviewing it against the same stale understanding would not have caught it. The fix is to regenerate the snapshot or validate the schema against production before generating, and to say plainly that the first three successes are not evidence the pipeline is reliable.
Ask the owner to verify every generated migration against production before running it, and make that a required review step. The process worked three times before.
Investigate whether the model hallucinated the table. If the table is in the snapshot it supplied, the behaviour is defensible given the input.
Add a step to the pipeline that lists every table the generated migration references, so the owner can see them all at once.

questions.explanation: The table is real — in the snapshot the pipeline was given. So this is **not a hallucination**, it is a validation environment that has drifted, and the consequence reaches further than this one migration: the first three successes were validated against the same stale snapshot and are therefore weaker evidence than they appear. Regenerating or revalidating against production addresses the actual defect, and being explicit about what the earlier successes prove is what keeps the team from over-trusting them.

whyWrong.B: The earlier successes make this option tempting, and it is the reason the team over-trusts the pipeline. A review by an owner working from the same understanding of the schema will not catch a table that exists in the snapshot and not in production.
whyWrong.C: The logs show the table was in the supplied input, so there is nothing to investigate on that axis. Calling it defensible given the input accepts the drift as normal, which is the condition that produced the problem.
whyWrong.D: Showing the table names in one place is a presentation improvement. It does not establish whether the tables exist in production, which is the question the owner was asking.

questions.mindset: When a generated artefact references something real but wrong, check the environment it was generated from before blaming the model.

questions.scenario: A platform team supports the internal issue-tracker integration for 200 engineers. It is configured centrally, it authenticates with per-engineer tokens from the company's identity provider, and it is scoped to read and comment but not to close or reopen issues. Four engineers have reported that they cannot perform a task they used to be able to do, and each has asked for the extra scope.

options.text: Route the exception through a named owner and a decision recorded against it, rather than granting the extra scope ad hoc. Each of the four has a real workflow gap, and the right response is to fix it — but least privilege means the grant is a decision with an owner, an expiry or a review point, and a record of why this person has it. Four individual ad-hoc grants become a pattern nobody can audit, and 'everyone on the team can close issues' is not the unit of permission.
Grant the four engineers the additional scope. They have a legitimate need, and the integration is internal, so the risk is low.
Refuse all four. The scope was set centrally for good reason, and a request for more scope is a signal to find a different way to do the task.
Grant the wider scope to the whole team. Four requests from one team suggests the original scope was set too narrowly for how the team works.

questions.explanation: Both facts are true: the requests are legitimate, and the current scope is deliberately narrow. The resolution is **an exception process rather than either granting or refusing** — a named owner, a recorded reason, and a review point, because an informal grant is indistinguishable from a policy change once four of them exist. That keeps the default least-privilege while making the exceptions visible, which is what an audit of this integration would ask about.

whyWrong.B: Granting individually without a record is how least privilege erodes in practice. Four engineers cannot be reviewed later, because nothing captures why each has it or whether the need still exists.
whyWrong.C: Refusing a legitimate workflow gap punishes the requesters and pushes the workaround somewhere less visible. A recorded exception achieves the control that the refusal was trying to achieve.
whyWrong.D: Four requests from one team is not evidence about the whole estate, and widening scope for everyone is the opposite of least privilege. This is the failure mode where an exception becomes a default without anyone deciding it was one.

questions.mindset: A legitimate request against a deliberate default is an exception to record with an owner, not a grant or a refusal to make informally.

questions.scenario: Lockridge Energy's platform team was asked to make the organisation's approved MCP servers available to engineers. The security team's constraint is that nothing unapproved may ever connect, and the platform team's constraint is that engineers should be able to add whichever approved server their work requires without a ticket. Twelve servers are approved; different teams need different subsets; the list changes a few times a year.
questions.stem: Which TWO design elements are necessary to satisfy both constraints? Choose TWO.

options.text: Publish the approved list centrally with each server's scope, and let engineers select from it at the scope their work needs. The list changes a few times a year, and a published set with a named owner is what makes that change cheap.

Put the boundary in a higher-precedence managed layer as a deny rule, so an unapproved server cannot connect regardless of what is added at project or user level. That is the only element that makes the security constraint true rather than documented.
Have the platform team add every approved server to every repository centrally, so uniformity removes the need for any per-engineer selection.
Document the approved list and let each team configure its own subset, with a quarterly audit of what has actually connected.

questions.explanation: The two constraints pull in opposite directions and both are satisfied only by **separating the list from the boundary**. A centrally published, scope-annotated set the platform team maintains gives engineers local selection without a ticket, and a managed deny rule at a precedence a repository cannot override is what makes 'nothing unapproved may ever connect' true rather than documented. That separation also survives the list changing, because updating the list does not mean re-establishing the boundary.

whyWrong.C: Uniformity removes selection but not the boundary — a repository can still add a server the list does not contain, and twelve servers for every engineer puts irrelevant tools in front of the model on every task. It also makes each list change a change to every repository.
whyWrong.D: Documentation constrains behaviour reliably until it is inconvenient, and quarterly auditing is detection rather than prevention: it produces a finding rather than a blocked connection. It is also the option that scales linearly and fails quietly at 200 engineers.

questions.mindset: Publish what is allowed centrally and let people choose within it — but put the boundary in a layer that cannot be overridden from below.

questions.scenario: Sandhurst Foods' engineers ask for the ability to run an agent that plans and executes a migration across four services autonomously overnight. The lead engineer's assessment is that the work is genuinely independent per service and that the tests confirm each conversion. The platform lead's assessment is that an unattended agent making changes across four services is a very large blast radius for work nobody is watching.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements are MOST defensible? Choose TWO.

options.text: Take both assessments as true and design around the conflict. The work is independent and testable, which is the case for unattended execution, and four services is a blast radius, which is the case against. The resolution is not 'autonomous or not' but 'how wide'.
Approve the autonomous run. The work is independent and the tests confirm each conversion, so the conditions for unattended execution are met.

Keep the autonomy and shrink the exposure: one service at a time, per-service verification before the next begins, each change reviewable on its own, and the run stopping at the first failure rather than continuing.
Approve the run but require a human to review the combined result the next morning. The independence of the work makes the sequencing safe.

questions.explanation: Both assessments are accurate and they are about **different properties** — independence and testability on one side, blast radius on the other — so the decision is a design question about width. One service at a time with per-service verification and a stop at the first failure keeps the reason for automating (the work is repetitive and independent) while bounding the cost of a wrong turn to one service. That answers the real tension rather than discarding half the evidence.

whyWrong.B: The testability argument justifies automating the conversions, and it says nothing about how many services should change before anyone looks. Accepting the run accepts both the good property and the bad one.
whyWrong.D: A morning review of a combined result is the worst of both: the exposure is unchanged and the review is now harder, because four services' worth of changes have to be understood together rather than one at a time.

questions.mindset: When independence justifies automation and scale justifies caution, keep the autonomy and shrink the exposure.

questions.scenario: Marbury Council's support lead is preparing an operational review for a regional director who has asked, in one sentence, what the team has done with the tooling. The team has four numbers: sessions per week, prompts written, documents produced, and the number of staff who used it at least once. It also has one anecdote: a manager who says it saved her two hours a week.
questions.stem: What is the MOST defensible answer?

options.text: Lead with the output measure and give the anecdote its proper weight. Documents produced is a count of work delivered; sessions and prompts are activity that could be explained by poor prompts; staff who used it once is reach, not value. The manager's two hours a week is the most informative number in the set precisely because it is stated by someone with a before and an after — and it is one person, so it should be offered as an indicative figure with the caveat attached, not as an organisation-wide saving.
Report all four numbers and the anecdote, and let the director weigh them. Completeness is the safest answer to a one-sentence request.
Report only the time saving, scaled to the team. The anecdote is the only figure that describes an outcome rather than an activity, and scaling it gives the director a usable number.
Report the session and prompt counts, because they are measurable and the anecdote cannot be verified. A regional director will not act on one person's recollection.

questions.explanation: The four numbers measure different things and only one of them is close to value. **Documents produced** counts delivered work; sessions and prompts measure activity and are equally consistent with poor prompting; people who used it once is reach. The time saving is the most informative because it has a before and an after attached to someone who knows their own work — and it is also the easiest to over-claim. Saying so, and giving it as an indicative figure, is what makes it usable rather than the number that got the team in trouble later.

whyWrong.B: Handing over four activity measures and one anecdote without a judgement puts the weighting on the director, who does not know what each number means. It also lets the two weakest numbers sit alongside the one strong one without distinction.
whyWrong.C: Scaling a single self-reported figure across a team converts one person's experience into an organisation-wide claim, which is exactly the number that will not survive scrutiny when the director asks how it was measured.
whyWrong.D: Measurability is not relevance. The counts are verifiable and they describe how much the tool was used, not what it produced — and the anecdote, properly caveated, is the only figure here that speaks to an outcome.

questions.mindset: Separate what was measured from what changed, and caveat the one strong number rather than scaling it.
